Preface
These are the lecture notes for FIN700, a mathematics camp for incoming PhD students in Finance. The camp builds the mathematical foundations used throughout the doctoral finance sequence, in three parts:

title: FIN700: Mathematics for PhD Finance
text:
How to read these notes
The material is developed from first principles and assumes only comfort with undergraduate calculus. Definitions, theorems, and worked examples are numbered by chapter for easy cross-reference. Numerical illustrations are produced with executable code cells, so every figure can be reproduced from source.

title: 1  Vectors and Vector Spaces
text:
1.1 Vector spaces
Linear algebra is, at its heart, the study of linear maps — functions between spaces that respect addition and scaling. Before we can talk about such maps, however, we need the spaces they act on. That is the job of this chapter: we build up the notion of a vector space .
Fix a positive integer \(n\). The set \(\mathbb{R}^n = \left\{ \boldsymbol{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) : x_i \in \mathbb{R} \right\}\) is the collection of all ordered lists of \(n\) real numbers. We call its elements vectors and write them in bold, \(\boldsymbol{x}\), reserving plain italics \(x_i\) for the individual components. By convention a vector is a column, \[
\boldsymbol{x} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{pmatrix},
\] and we write \(\boldsymbol{x}^\top = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) for the corresponding row when it is convenient to save space on the page.
Two operations make \(\mathbb{R}^n\) more than a bare set. We can add two vectors component-wise, \[
\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y} = (x_1 + y_1, \dots, x_n + y_n),
\] and we can scale a vector by a real number \(\alpha\) (a scalar), \[
\alpha \boldsymbol{x} = (\alpha x_1, \dots, \alpha x_n).
\] Both results are again vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Combining the two operations gives the single most important construction in the subject.
In finance, a portfolio can be expressed as a linear combination. If \(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_k\) are the return vectors of \(k\) assets and \(w_1, \dots, w_k\) are portfolio weights,then \[
\boldsymbol{r}_{\text{p}} = w_1 \boldsymbol{r}_1 + \cdots + w_k \boldsymbol{r}_k
\] is the return vector of the portfolio.
The list looks long, but every axiom simply says that addition and scaling behave the way the notation already tempts you to assume. One checks directly that \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with the componentwise operations above, satisfies all eight; it is the prototype we keep in mind. The value of the abstract definition is that it is satisfied by many other sets as well.
Inside a vector space, the interesting subsets are those that are themselves closed under the two operations — take a linear combination of members and you never leave the subset.
Spanning asks whether a list is large enough to reach every vector. The complementary question is whether it is efficient — whether any vector is redundant, expressible through the others.
Independence is exactly what makes representations unique, which is the property we actually care about.

title: 1  Vectors and Vector Spaces
text:
Definition 1.1 A linear combination of vectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{v}_k\) is any vector of the form \[
\alpha_1 \boldsymbol{v}_1 + \alpha_2 \boldsymbol{v}_2 + \cdots + \alpha_k \boldsymbol{v}_k,
\qquad \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}.
\]



Definition 1.2 A vector space (over \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a set \(V\) on which two binary operations are defined:

addition: \[
\text{if } \boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \in V \text{, then } \boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v} \in V
\]
scalar multiplication: \[
\text{if } \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{u} \in V \text{, then } \alpha \boldsymbol{u} \in V
\]

which satisfy the following axioms:

\((\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v}) + \boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{u} + (\boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{w})\).
\(\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{u}\).
There exists \(\boldsymbol{0} \in V\), such that \(\boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{0} = \boldsymbol{v}\).
For all \(\boldsymbol{v}\), there exists \(-\boldsymbol{v} \in V\) with \(\boldsymbol{v} + (-\boldsymbol{v}) = \boldsymbol{0}\).
\(\alpha(\beta \boldsymbol{v}) = (\alpha\beta)\boldsymbol{v}\).
\(1\,\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{v}\).
\(\alpha(\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v}) = \alpha\boldsymbol{u} + \alpha\boldsymbol{v}\).
\((\alpha + \beta)\boldsymbol{v} = \alpha\boldsymbol{v} + \beta\boldsymbol{v}\).





Definition 1.3 A subset \(W \subseteq V\) is a subspace if it is nonempty and closed under addition and scalar multiplication: whenever \(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \in W\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), both \(\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v} \in W\) and \(\alpha \boldsymbol{u} \in W\).


Definition 1.4 The span of \(\boldsymbol{v}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{v}_k\) is the set of all their linear combinations, \[
\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{v}_k)
  = \{ \alpha_1 \boldsymbol{v}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_k \boldsymbol{v}_k : \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R} \}.
\] If this set is all of \(V\), we say the vectors span \(V\).



Definition 1.5 The vectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{v}_k\) are linearly independent if the only linear combination equal to \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is the trivial one: \[
\alpha_1 \boldsymbol{v}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_k \boldsymbol{v}_k = \boldsymbol{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha_1 = \cdots = \alpha_k = 0.
\] Otherwise they are linearly dependent, and some vector among them is a linear combination of the rest.



Example 1.1 In linear regression \(y=\boldsymbol{X}\beta\), we always want to avoid perfect multicollinearity, a situation where the exogenous variables \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly dependent. For example, if there is a constant in the regression, the maximum number of dummy variables for a \(N\)-category variable is \(N-1\). Otherwise, the summation of dummies is equal to 1 (the constant).


Theorem 1.1 If \(\boldsymbol{v}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{v}_k\) are linearly independent, then every vector in their span is a linear combination of them in exactly one way.


Proof. Suppose some \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in the span had two representations, \[
\boldsymbol{x} = \sum_i \alpha_i \boldsymbol{v}_i = \sum_i \beta_i \boldsymbol{v}_i.
\] Subtracting gives \(\sum_i (\alpha_i - \beta_i)\boldsymbol{v}_i = \boldsymbol{0}\). By independence, \(\alpha_i = \beta_i\) for all \(i\); the two representations coincide.


Definition 1.6 A basis of vector space \(V\) is a list of vectors that is linearly independent and spans \(V\).


Example 1.2 In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the standard basis is \(\boldsymbol{e}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{e}_n\), where \(\boldsymbol{e}_i\) has a \(1\) in position \(i\) and \(0\) elsewhere. For example, in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the standard basis is \([1,0]', [0,1]'\).
